craft_claim: Turning inward to evaluate one's own past conduct and revise policy on the basis of that evaluation is attested in ancient India's most public genre: Ashoka's Kalinga edict makes a ruler's first-person reflection on the consequences of his actions the engine of his proclamation.

supporting_evidence.location: Major Rock Edict XIII (Kalinga edict); Hultzsch 1925 ed. and trans., p. 43 (public domain); associated policy statements
supporting_evidence.note: The edict narrates Ashoka's earlier conquest-mindedness, his reckoning of the war's human cost, remorse, and the turn to conquest by dhamma — private evaluation of one's own past action staged as the reason for public change (paraphrased; no inscription text reproduced). The Kalinga campaign falls in Ashoka's eighth regnal year (conventionally c. 262-261 BCE, verified 2026-09-24); the edicts name the king 'Devanampiya Priyadasi'.

supporting_evidence.location: chapters on the Kalinga campaign, the edicts, and their interpretation
supporting_evidence.note: Thapar's scholarly study analyzes the edicts' composition, the Kalinga campaign, and Ashoka's self-presentation, providing the historical anchor for reading the edict's reflective self-evaluation critically rather than at face value.

counterevidence.note: The edict is state proclamation as well as introspection: the remorse narrative legitimates Mauryan dhamma policy, and a skeptical reading treats the reflection as political rhetoric rather than evidence of private motive. The tone-analogue survives (the genre performs inward evaluation); the biographical claim does not.

scope: Cross-cultural historical attestation that the reflective gesture (inward evaluation of personal past conduct) is not exclusively modern or Western; feeds card section 8.
exceptions: Public, rule-voiced reflection differs from the tone's default private address; cite as attestation of the attitude, not as a model of narrator voice.
